title: Lists and indexing
goals: Distinguish a list index from the value stored at that position
Read and update an item using a valid index
Trace a loop through list values and test an empty list
vocabulary: An integer position used to access an item
The number of items in a collection
One value stored in a collection
An error raised when an index is outside a sequence

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
counts = [4, 7, 4]
total = 0
for count in counts:
    total = total + count
print(total)

This fresh script prints 15. for count in counts supplies the stored values, not the indices. Both copies of 4 are processed because both are items. For an empty list written [], the body runs zero times and total stays 0. For [7], it runs once and prints 7.

blocks.label: Change only the list to [2, 0, 5]. Trace the three additions and state the final output. Explain why the middle item is processed even though its value is zero.

guided_practice.title: Trace an update
guided_practice.prompt: Start with counts = [4, 7, 4]. Run counts[0] = 6. Write the resulting list, its length and the value at index 2. Predict before running.
guided_practice.answer: The result is [6, 7, 4]; length remains 3; index 2 still holds 4. Only the first item was replaced.

independent_case.title: Distinguish a value from an index
independent_case.task: Predict the three outputs. If the second print uses values[3] instead, where does execution stop and which later output is not produced?
independent_case.answer: Outputs are 9,2,3. With values[3], the first print produces 9, then IndexError occurs; the final length print is not reached. Positive valid indices are 0,1,2.

misconceptions: Length is the last nonnegative index
Length counts items; the last nonnegative index of a nonempty list is one less.
A loop variable always contains an index
A direct list loop supplies stored values.
Updating one item grows the list
Assignment at an existing index replaces that item; length is unchanged.
Repeated values are processed only once
Each position contributes one item, even when values repeat.

blocks.title: Positions and stored counts
blocks.caption: Equal stored values do not imply equal positions. There is no item at index 3.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
counts = [4, 7, 4]
print(len(counts))
print(counts[0])
print(counts[1])
counts[1] = 9
print(counts)

The printed lines are 3, 4, 7 and [4, 9, 4]. The assignment counts[1] = 9 replaces the item at index 1; it does not add a fourth item or change the two other values. The length stays 3. A recorded count can be changed by code without proving that the physical tray really contains that many objects.
